strengths: The paper is well motivated: existing style-personalization methods mostly rely on diffusion backbones and per-style fine-tuning, and this work targets the more efficient scale-wise AR regime (Infinity), a timely and under-explored setting.

The analysis in Sec. 4 is the most valuable part: the step-wise prompt-injection study (Fig. 2) and the SVD-based dominant-singular-component experiment (Fig. 3), extended in the supplementary with top-k sweeps (Figs. 7-8), provide an empirical, reasonably careful basis for the design of PFB.

Both proposed modules are lightweight and training-free: PFB (exponential spectral reweighting + blending, Eq. 5-6) and SAC (content-path Q/K injection, Eq. 7) are simple, clearly formulated, and well explained, with an algorithmic summary in the supplementary.

Evaluation follows the established FineStyle protocol with 8 baselines, reports a harmonic metric, includes an ablation (Tab. 2) and alpha sensitivity study (Tab. 3), and a 30-participant user study (Tab. 4).

Generalization beyond the primary backbone is demonstrated qualitatively on Infinity-8B and Switti (Fig. 12), and a text-only style-aligned mode is shown (Fig. 14); limitations are explicitly discussed (heterogeneous/conflicting styles).
Reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation and baseline setup descriptions, including official/unofficial code sources for all comparison methods.
weaknesses: Headline empirical advantage is marginal or absent: the proposed harmonic score of the method (0.437) is essentially tied with, and numerically slightly below, StyleAligned (0.438), while style fidelity Simg (0.630) is clearly below IP-Adapter (0.763) and StyleAR (0.701). The primary quantitative selling point is prompt fidelity, and the main practical advantage is inference speed rather than quality.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work the paper itself cites: spectral manipulation for style transfer dates back to WCT [28,33], content-style decomposition in VAR models already exists (CSD-VAR [34]), and training-free style alignment on scale-wise AR models was explored in [37]; SAC (copying content-path Q/K) closely mirrors established shared-attention / PnP-style techniques [18,52,53].

The central claim that the dominant singular component encodes 'style' rests on stylized-to-color prompt pairs ('red truck' vs 'purple cat'), which confounds style with color/texture attributes; the analysis does not demonstrate the separation holds for complex artistic styles used in the actual benchmark.

The step-wise analysis is correlational: inferring that step 2/F3 governs content and style from CLIP similarity of prompt-swap outputs is indirect, and CLIP-based metrics (Stxt, Simg) are known to be noisy proxies for style transfer quality, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The dual-stream design roughly doubles the compute of the backbone, yet comparison of inference times against tuning-based methods includes their tuning time, which inflates the reported speed advantage in a somewhat favorable framing.

The user study is small (30 participants) with a forced-choice among five systems; no statistical significance is reported, and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the method itself (only baseline setups are documented).

strengths: The core analysis (Sec. 4) is a thoughtful empirical study: the step-wise prompt-injection experiment (Fig. 2) and the SVD manipulation experiment (Fig. 3, supplementary Figs. 7-8) are simple but well-designed interventions that support the claim that the dominant singular component of F3 encodes style-like attributes.

The proposed method is fully training-free and very fast (3.58 s per 1024x1024 image on an A6000), and the dual-stream design with Principal Feature Blending and Structural Attention Correction is a reasonable, well-motivated realization of the analysis findings.

The ablation study (Tab. 2) is sensible: it separates direct feature replacement (REP) from SVD-based blending, showing the expected trade-off between style fidelity and content leakage, and supplementary ablations over alpha and top-k singular values reinforce the spectral analysis.

Generalization to other scale-wise AR models (Infinity-8B, Switti in Fig. 12) and the text-only style-aligned extension (Fig. 14) provide some evidence of plug-and-play applicability beyond the main backbone.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative results do not actually support a claim of superiority. In Tab. 1, StyleAligned achieves a higher harmonic score (0.438) than the proposed method (0.437), and both IP-Adapter (0.763) and StyleAligned (0.716) achieve much higher style fidelity. The gains on prompt fidelity (0.334 vs. 0.324) are marginal, with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported. The paper characterizes this as 'competitive,' but the empirical advantage over existing training-free methods is essentially nil.

The evaluation relies exclusively on CLIP-based metrics (Stxt, Simg), which the paper itself admits can be misleading due to content leakage and mode collapse. No complementary quantitative measures (e.g., FID-style metrics, style-classifier accuracy, or human evaluation beyond the single user study) are provided to triangulate.

The central analysis conflates 'style' with 'color.' The style pair set Tsty is constructed solely by changing colors ('red truck' vs. 'green truck'), and the SVD analysis measures color-related CLIP similarity. Color is only one narrow component of artistic style (texture, brushwork, palette, composition). The claim that the dominant singular component 'encodes style' is therefore over-generalized from a color-only proxy.

The user study is small (30 participants), and the comparison set was curated by the authors to exclude baselines such as StyleAR and CSGO; the reported preferences (35.3% vs. 32.0%) are close and provide weak evidence.

Several methodological choices are under-justified. The key step is fixed at s=3 based on experiments on a specific model and prompt sets; the sensitivity of the pipeline to this choice is not analyzed. SAC is borrowed from attention-swapping ideas well established in diffusion models (Plug-and-Play, StyleAligned), so its novelty is limited, and its contribution in the ablation is small (+0.011 harmonic).

Figure 3 (the pivotal evidence for the SVD claim) is very hard to read: the bar-chart panels are small, the axis labels are illegible, and the quantitative deltas being interpreted are not clearly visible, weakening the evidentiary weight of a central claim.

The overall contribution feels incremental: exponential singular-value reweighting is closely related to classical feature transforms (WCT, AdaIN line of work, which the paper itself cites), and combining spectral reweighting with attention swapping on an existing AR backbone yields results statistically indistinguishable from prior training-free methods.
Writing quality issues (e.g., 'To analysis this', inconsistent notation in Fig. 3, dense Sec. 4) reduce clarity in the sections that carry the paper's analytical claims.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely interesting empirical analysis of scale-wise autoregressive generation models: the step-wise prompt-injection experiment (Fig. 2) and the SVD-based decomposition of F3 (Fig. 3, supplemented by the top-k analysis in Fig. 7-8) are well-designed diagnostics that convincingly localize style information in the dominant singular component of the third-scale feature. This analysis is the strongest part of the paper and could be useful beyond the specific method.

The proposed method is fully training-free and lightweight, and the efficiency claim is well supported: 3.58s per 1024x1024 image vs. tens to hundreds of seconds for tuning-based baselines, with implementation details and baseline configurations reported in the appendix for reproducibility.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: eight baselines spanning training-free and tuning-based paradigms, the FineStyle benchmark protocol, ablations over both components (Tab. 2), the decay rate alpha (Tab. 3), top-k singular values, a user study (30 participants), and qualitative generalization to Infinity-8B and Switti (Fig. 12).

The paper is honest about limitations (e.g., heterogeneous/mixed styles in Sec. E) and reports metrics (Simg) where it does not lead, which improves credibility compared to papers claiming uniform superiority.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative result is essentially a tie, not an improvement: the harmonic score is 0.437 vs. 0.438 for StyleAligned, and style fidelity (0.630) is well below IP-Adapter (0.763) and StyleAligned (0.716). No statistical significance, variance, or confidence intervals are reported across the 190 prompts x 10 styles, so the claimed 'competitive style fidelity and prompt fidelity' rests on differences within likely noise. The paper's framing as 'competitive' is fair, but the contribution then leans heavily on speed and analysis rather than demonstrated quality gains.

The dual-stream architecture roughly doubles the compute of the underlying Infinity backbone relative to a single-stream inference, which is not discussed or ablated; the speed comparison is favorable only because diffusion baselines are slow. A comparison against a single-pass AR variant (e.g., a style-prompt-only or weaker injection baseline) would clarify the cost-benefit trade-off.

Several methodological choices are heuristic and only weakly justified: the exponential decay weighting in Eq. (5) is ad hoc (alpha=1.0 chosen empirically with modest differences across settings), and the SAC module of replacing generation Q/K with content-path Q/K is a close analogue of shared-attention ideas from StyleAligned [18] and PnP-style guidance [48, 52, 53], so the novelty of the second module is limited.

The analysis relies on CLIP-based similarity metrics, which are known to be noisy proxies for style and content fidelity; the paper itself acknowledges that Simg can be misleading (content leakage), yet the key findings in Sec. 4 are quantified with the same CLIP measures. Perceptual or human-validated evidence for the step-2/F3 finding is not provided.

Some claims are under-supported by the reported evidence: the generalization to Switti and Infinity-8B is qualitative only (no metrics), the user study includes only five methods and 30 participants without significance testing, and it is unclear how robust the 'pivotal step' finding is across backbones with different scale counts.

Presentation issues: the mapping between analysis notation (F3) and the pipeline notation (F_sty_3, F_gen_3) requires effort to trace; Eq. (6) mixes styles and content in a way that is hard to parse without Algorithm 1; and Fig. 3's heatmap is difficult to read. These are presentation refinements rather than material flaws.

Overall, the contribution is an increment: a well-executed adaptation of known intervention ideas (feature injection, attention replacement) to a new backbone family, with an appealing but empirically demonstrated-rather-than-theoretically-grounded SVD observation. The lack of a clear quantitative win over existing training-free methods places it near the acceptance boundary.
